distillation_scope: Pure disease-name leaf distillation for the full clinical spectrum of vertebral osteomyelitis, including hematogenous, contiguous, and procedure-associated disease without splitting by organism.

latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Viable organisms reach vertebral endplates, adjacent disc, or paravertebral tissue by bacteremia, endocarditis embolic spread, urinary or gastrointestinal bacteremia, skin/soft-tissue source, injection drug use, prior spine procedure, contiguous infection, or rarely direct inoculation.
Microbial growth in vertebral cancellous bone and endplates causes marrow edema, pain, local inflammatory response, osteolysis, and progressive structural injury.
Spread across adjacent endplates and intervertebral disc produces spondylodiscitis and exposes epidural, paraspinal, psoas, prevertebral, and foraminal spaces to infection.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Local pyogenic inflammation and bone destruction
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Neutrophilic inflammation, cytokine signaling, proteolysis, edema, and vascular congestion amplify pain, CRP/ESR rise, vertebral destruction, and risk of collapse or instability.
Fever, tachycardia, leukocyte change, thrombocytosis or thrombocytopenia, anemia of inflammation, CRP/ESR rise, and possible sepsis physiology from deep infection and bloodstream involvement.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Epidural, paraspinal, and psoas abscess extension
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Infection extends beyond bone/disc into epidural phlegmon or abscess, paraspinal soft tissue, psoas, prevertebral tissue, or foramina; this creates source-control problems and compression risk.

Epidural collection, canal stenosis, vertebral collapse, foraminal inflammation, or direct inflammatory injury impairs roots, cauda equina, or spinal cord and causes radicular pain, weakness, sensory loss, gait impairment, or bowel/bladder dysfunction.

latent_mechanisms.display_name: Persistent source, abscess, endovascular nidus, or hardware biofilm
latent_mechanisms.clinical_meaning: Undrained abscess, infected endocarditis vegetation, retained spinal hardware, inadequate antibiotic activity, resistant organism, or delayed diagnosis maintains microbial burden and relapse risk.

mechanism_edges.clinical_rationale: Vertebral marrow infection requires organisms to reach the spinal endplate or adjacent vertebral tissue.
Endplate infection often spreads across the disc space to adjacent vertebral endplates.
Active infection in bone drives local inflammatory edema, pain, osteolysis, and acute-phase markers.
MRI/CT vertebral marrow and endplate abnormalities are the imaging expression of vertebral infection.
Spondylodiscitis produces disc-space signal abnormality or enhancement.
Contiguous spread from disc/endplate can enter epidural or paraspinal compartments.
Inflamed vertebral bone, disc, and paraspinal tissue produce focal neck, thoracic, or back pain.
Pain severity tracks local inflammatory burden, mechanical instability, and neural irritation.
Mechanical loading and straight-leg raise can aggravate infected spine pain.
Focal vertebral inflammation can produce midline or paraspinal tenderness.
CRP usually rises in active vertebral osteomyelitis and falls with control.
ESR is commonly elevated and often remains high in subacute spinal infection.
Persistent osteolysis and endplate destruction can produce deformity, collapse, and instability.
Fever is common but may be absent, especially in chronic disease or older/immunosuppressed patients.
Recurrent or intermittent fever is often more informative than a single triage temperature.
Deep infection may produce sweats despite absent measured fever.
Fever, pain, and systemic inflammation cause tachycardia.
Leukocytosis may occur, but WBC can be normal in chronic, elderly, or immunosuppressed presentations.
Inflammation can cause thrombocytosis, while severe sepsis or comorbidity can lower platelets.
Chronic inflammation and comorbidity can produce anemia.
High-burden infection with bacteremia or source-control failure can progress to shock.
Epidural extension appears on MRI as abscess, phlegmon, or enhancing collection.
Early epidural inflammatory tissue may be described as phlegmon before a fully drainable abscess forms.
Contiguous soft-tissue extension produces paraspinal, prevertebral, or foraminal abscess.
Lumbar infection can extend into the psoas or iliopsoas compartment.
Abscess extension determines measurable collection size.
Epidural, paraspinal, psoas, or prevertebral collections may require drainage or decompression beyond antibiotics.
Epidural or foraminal extension can compress neural structures and trigger urgent deficits.
Nerve-root irritation produces shooting pain, paresthesia, or dermatomal symptoms.
Cord, cauda equina, or root compromise manifests as neurologic deficit.
Motor pathway or root compromise lowers limb strength.
Root, cord, or cauda equina involvement produces numbness, paresthesia, or sensory level.
Cauda equina or severe spinal canal compromise can impair bowel or bladder control.
Pain and weakness impair ambulation.
Epidural collection or destructive deformity narrows the spinal canal.
Imaging mass effect on thecal sac, cord, or cauda equina is the structural correlate of neurologic compromise.
Active neural compression raises hazard of progression or persistent neurologic injury.
Retained abscess, endocarditis, or infected hardware increases the need for procedural source control.
A persistent nidus means source control is incomplete.
Undrained foci, hardware, and inadequate active therapy increase relapse.
Persistent abscess activity can enlarge or seed additional deep collections.
Endovascular or undrained foci can sustain bloodstream positivity.
Resistance, atypical organisms, and inadequate empiric regimen reduce effective coverage.
Endocarditis can be either the source of VO by hematogenous spread or a concurrent bacteremic nidus.
Urinary tract infection or recurrent gram-negative bacteremia can seed vertebrae.
Enteric pathogens may reach the spine after gastrointestinal infection or bacteremia.
Recent injection, surgery, or instrumentation changes prior probability and source-control context.
Mortality is usually mediated by sepsis, neurologic catastrophe, uncontrolled source, comorbidity, or endocarditis rather than pain alone.

axes.shape_free_text: Focal neck, thoracic, lumbar, sacral, or low-back pain compatible with vertebral osteomyelitis.
Severity of spinal pain, including inability to ambulate, severe persistent pain, or acute worsening on chronic pain.
Duration of focal spinal pain before current evaluation; may be acute, subacute, or many months.
Pain worsened by movement, axial loading, straight-leg raise, position change, or walking.
Focal vertebral or paraspinal tenderness on examination.
Radiating limb pain, shooting pain, paresthesia, or dermatomal irritation from foraminal, epidural, or root involvement.
Any objective focal neurologic deficit, including weakness, sensory loss, myelopathy, cauda equina syndrome, or gait deficit.
Lower-extremity motor weakness or reduced measured strength due to spinal cord, cauda equina, or root involvement.
Numbness, paresthesia, dermatomal sensory loss, or sensory level.
New bowel or bladder dysfunction from cauda equina or severe spinal canal compromise.
Impaired ambulation from pain, weakness, myelopathy, or radiculopathy.
Subjective or documented fever history across the illness, including intermittent fever or recurrent fever admissions.
Night sweats or inflammatory sweats accompanying deep infection.
Diarrhea or enteric illness that can contextualize enteric bacteremia but is not required for VO.
Measured body temperature at clinical snapshot.
Measured heart rate.
Measured respiratory rate.
Peripheral oxygen saturation.
Measured systolic blood pressure.
Mean arterial pressure measured or derived from blood pressure.
Peripheral white blood cell count, which can be high or normal in VO.
Peripheral neutrophil fraction.
Hemoglobin, which may fall with chronic inflammation or comorbidity.
Platelet count, which may rise with inflammation or fall with sepsis, medications, or comorbidity.
C-reactive protein; often elevated and useful for treatment response.
ESR; commonly elevated in subacute and chronic VO.
Serum creatinine, reflecting background kidney disease, sepsis-associated AKI, or antimicrobial toxicity context.
AST, used as baseline illness and antimicrobial toxicity context rather than a core VO marker.
ALT, used as baseline illness and antimicrobial toxicity context rather than a core VO marker.
Serum sodium; may reflect comorbidity, inflammation, dehydration, or sepsis context.
MRI/CT evidence of vertebral marrow, endplate, or bone infection compatible with VO.
Disc-space infection or spondylodiscitis on MRI/CT.
Spinal epidural abscess or epidural collection associated with VO.
Enhancing epidural inflammatory tissue or phlegmon without a mature drainable abscess.
Paraspinal, prevertebral, foraminal, or adjacent soft-tissue abscess associated with VO.
Psoas or iliopsoas abscess associated with lumbar VO.
Largest reported diameter of epidural, paraspinal, psoas, or prevertebral abscess when measured.
Canal narrowing from epidural collection, phlegmon, deformity, or pre-existing stenosis worsened by VO.
MRI/CT evidence of thecal sac, cord, cauda equina, or root compression.
Endplate erosion, collapse, deformity, instability, or pathologic fracture risk caused by VO.

Clinical course context of persistent or recurrent bacteremia suggesting an endovascular or undrained source. Case culture results should be recorded in confirmatory_findings, not ordinary observations.
Probability that blood cultures identify the organism; use in confirmatory_findings, not ordinary case observations.
Probability that bone, disc, epidural, psoas, or paraspinal sample culture identifies the organism; confirmatory only.
Probability that 16S rRNA PCR or other molecular testing detects pathogen from spinal or adjacent tissue; confirmatory only.
Probability that pathology from bone, disc, or epidural tissue confirms acute/chronic osteomyelitis or abscess tissue; confirmatory only.
Probability that the antimicrobial regimen is active against the causative organism with adequate exposure for VO.
Probability that chosen therapy has adequate bone/disc penetration and duration for VO.
Concurrent or source infective endocarditis identified clinically or by echocardiography.
Largest vegetation size on echocardiography when endocarditis is present.
Clinically detected murmur that may support endocarditis or structural valve disease context.
Probability that urinary tract infection or urinary bacteremia is the source context for VO.
Probability that enteric infection, gastrointestinal translocation, or enteric bacteremia is the source context for VO.
Recent or repeated spinal injection, nerve block, surgery, instrumentation, or invasive procedure exposure.
Steroids, transplant immunosuppression, neutropenia, malignancy therapy, advanced HIV, or other impaired host defense context.
Need for drainage, debridement, decompression, stabilization, hardware removal, or valve/device source control.
Adequacy of source control after any needed drainage, debridement, decompression, stabilization, hardware removal, or endocarditis intervention.
Hazard of new or worsening neurologic injury from epidural abscess, canal compression, or spinal instability.
Hazard of collapse, pathologic fracture, deformity, or mechanical instability from destructive VO.
Hazard of abscess enlargement, inadequate drainage, persistent deep infection, or new contiguous collection.
Hazard of relapse after apparent improvement, especially with short therapy, inadequate activity, retained source, abscess, or hardware.
Hazard of septic shock from high-burden bacteremia, uncontrolled source, or severe host vulnerability.
Hazard from concomitant or source endocarditis: valve failure, embolization, persistent bacteremia, or device infection.
Lifespan mortality hazard for vertebral osteomyelitis, mediated by septic shock, neurologic catastrophe, uncontrolled abscess/source, endocarditis, major comorbidity, or treatment toxicity.

axis_couplings.conditionality: When pain is mechanically provoked rather than purely radicular.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Severe spinal inflammatory pain often co-varies with movement-provoked pain.

axis_couplings.conditionality: ESR may lag CRP during improvement.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Both track inflammatory burden, with ESR slower to normalize.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Risk is amplified by canal stenosis, compression, cervical/thoracic location, or neurologic symptoms.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Epidural abscess is the major pathway to neurologic decline.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Deficits may precede imaging if compression develops rapidly.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Mass effect on neural structures causes objective deficits.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Driven by severe cord/cauda equina compromise, respiratory failure in cervical disease, or inability to control epidural source.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Severe neurologic compromise marks advanced disease and procedural urgency.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Risk rises with extensive bony destruction, deformity, osteoporosis, or delayed treatment.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Structural destruction creates instability and fracture hazard.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Need without adequate drainage/decompression is the high-risk state.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Persistent drainable or compressive foci can progress despite antibiotics.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Only applies when adequate active antimicrobial therapy is also present.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Effective source control reduces persistent nidus and relapse.
Active therapy lowers burden and relapse risk.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Especially if vegetation is large, valve/device source remains, or antibiotics are inactive.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Endocarditis can sustain bacteremia and seed VO.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Amplified by large vegetation, severe regurgitation, prosthetic material, or persistent cultures.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Endocarditis changes outcome through embolic and valve-failure hazards.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Applies to severe acute bacteremic or uncontrolled-source presentations.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Shock is a direct mortality pathway.
Valve failure, embolization, and persistent endovascular infection raise mortality.

axis_couplings.conditionality: Highest when combined with bacteremia, sepsis, or neurologic compromise.
axis_couplings.clinical_rationale: Uncontrolled deep infection is a route to sepsis and irreversible injury.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Empiric therapy only reshapes infection if it covers the causative organism.
Renal dysfunction changes dosing and nephrotoxicity risk.

side_effects.interpretation: Vancomycin, aminoglycosides, or severe illness can worsen kidney function.

treatments.context_specific_role: Initial active coverage while organism, susceptibility, source, and surgical need are being clarified.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Definitive therapy depends on organism identity, susceptibility, and adequate dosing.
Antibiotic-only therapy is less reliable with retained abscess, endocarditis, or hardware nidus.

failure_modes: inadequate oral bioavailability or bone penetration

side_effects.interpretation: Several prolonged antimicrobial regimens can cause hepatotoxicity.

treatments.context_specific_role: Organism- and susceptibility-directed therapy over the duration needed for bone infection.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Oral step-down is more reliable when deep source control is adequate and the patient is clinically stable.
Improving inflammatory markers support transition to oral therapy.
Compressive or uncontrolled epidural disease should not be treated as simple step-down context.

failure_modes: worsening CRP, pain, or neurologic signs

side_effects.interpretation: Oral agents can cause hepatotoxicity or drug interactions depending on regimen.

treatments.context_specific_role: Continuation phase once active organism-directed therapy, stability, and source context permit.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Procedural source control only helps when there is a drainable, compressive, unstable, or debridable target.
Neurologic compromise makes decompression more time-sensitive.
A larger or accessible collection is more likely to benefit from drainage.

failure_modes: no drainable or surgically reachable target
procedure delayed after irreversible neurologic injury
additional source such as endocarditis remains

side_effects.interpretation: Procedure complications can rarely create residual collection or wound infection.

treatments.context_specific_role: Drainage/debridement/decompression when abscess, neurologic compromise, deformity, instability, or failure of medical therapy creates a source-control problem.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Bracing and activity restriction matter most when mechanical instability risk is present.

failure_modes: sedation or immobility complications from analgesic strategy

side_effects.interpretation: Excess immobility or sedating analgesia can worsen function temporarily.

treatments.context_specific_role: Mechanical and pain support while antimicrobial and source-control treatments act.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Valve/device intervention only addresses an endovascular source when present.
Valve failure, embolic risk, or persistent endovascular infection increases benefit.

side_effects.interpretation: Perioperative risk exists but can be outweighed by source control when endocarditis is driving hazard.

treatments.context_specific_role: Endovascular source control when VO is linked to active endocarditis, valve destruction, prosthetic material, or device infection.

effect_modifiers.clinical_rationale: Hemodynamic support matters when shock or organ dysfunction is present or imminent.

failure_modes: persistent shock if source control or active antibiotics are delayed
fluid overload in renal or cardiac disease

side_effects.interpretation: Fluid overload can worsen oxygenation in susceptible patients.

treatments.context_specific_role: Physiologic support for severe VO with sepsis while definitive antimicrobial and source-control pathways take effect.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises prior probability and worsens reserve; fever and WBC response may be blunted.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Older patients can present afebrile despite deep infection.
Frailty and comorbidity raise mortality from sepsis, surgery, and neurologic complications.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises invasive infection risk, bacteremia risk, renal toxicity context, and complication hazard.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: CKD shifts creatinine background independently of VO.
Poor reserve increases severe infection hazard.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises probability of unusual organisms, subacute presentation, bacteremia, and abscess progression while blunting fever.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Steroids or immunosuppression define this context.
Steroids can blunt fever.
Reduced host control can permit focal extension.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises direct inoculation or hardware-associated source probability and may change source-control need.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Spinal injection or instrumentation is directly represented as risk context.
Foreign material or procedure-associated nidus can sustain infection.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises hematogenous seeding probability, persistent source failure, and mortality through valve/embolic hazards.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Endocarditis is a major VO source context.
Persistent bacteremia increases spinal seeding and relapse risk.
Concomitant endocarditis creates a separate outcome hazard.

present.trajectory_modulation: Raises source-specific prior without converting VO into a pathogen subtype.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: UTI or recurrent urinary bacteremia supports urinary source context.
Enteric illness or bacteremia supports gastrointestinal source context.

present.trajectory_modulation: Prolongs pain, bone destruction, abscess extension, and relapse risk.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Delayed diagnosis is expressed as prolonged pain duration.
Untreated infection has more time to extend.
Inactive or short therapy increases relapse.

present.trajectory_modulation: Does not define a separate disease leaf; it reshapes source-control urgency and outcome hazard.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Abscess, deficit, or instability increases procedural need.
Compressive disease drives neurologic hazard.
Severe neurologic or structural disease increases mortality and procedural risk.

present.trajectory_modulation: Changes active coverage and diagnostic delay rather than defining the first-level leaf.

axis_response_modulation.clinical_rationale: Unusual or resistant pathogens are more likely to be missed by empiric regimens.
Delayed active therapy sustains burden.

supportive_care.clinical_rationale: Motor, sensory, gait, and bowel/bladder changes determine urgency of decompression.
MRI defines vertebral, disc, epidural, and paraspinal disease; early MRI can be falsely negative.
Source context changes antibiotic selection, duration, recurrence risk, and need for valve/device or abscess source control.
Blood cultures and image-guided biopsy guide definitive therapy; in severe sepsis or neurologic compression treatment should not be delayed.
Inflammatory marker trajectory and functional recovery expose treatment failure or relapse.
VO often requires prolonged antimicrobials; kidney and liver toxicity can change feasible regimens.
Pain, weakness, bracing, and hospitalization reduce mobility even after infection control begins.

quality_notes: No treatment ranking-label fields are used.
Culture, PCR, and pathology axes are defined for confirmatory_findings; case files should not place them in ordinary observations.
